43361: The parable of the tenants reuses Isaiah's vineyard song against the leaders of Jesus' day.
43363: 'Everyone under his vine and fig tree, with none to make them afraid.'
43364: The fruit of the vine and the kingdom feast
43365: Wine looks ahead to the messianic banquet. Herod's temple had a great golden vine over its entrance (described by Josephus), so the image was very public.
43366: Noah's vineyard (Gen 9:20), the cupbearer's dream (Gen 40:9-11), spies' huge cluster (Num 13:23), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:12-13), Naboth's vineyard (1 Kgs 21:1), useless vine wood (Ezek 15:2-6), vine of Sodom (Deut 32:32).
43367: Labourers in the vineyard (Matt 20:1-16), wicked tenants (Mark 12:1-9), the barren fig in a vineyard (Luke 13:6), the true vine (John 15:1), the grape harvest of judgement (Rev 14:18-20).
43368: Vine imagery can be comforting (abiding) and severe (pruning, burning). Reading only one side distorts it.
43373: Figs were a staple fruit, and the fig tree stood for peace and prosperity, and for Israel's fruitfulness or lack of it. Jesus' cursing of a fruitless fig tree, wrapped around his action in the temple, is widely read as an acted warning against the temple establishment.
43375: Sitting under vine and fig tree.
43377: God found Israel like early figs; Jeremiah's good and bad figs; Jesus' parable of the barren fig tree given one more year.
43379: Mark sandwiches the temple clearing between the cursing and the withered tree. Most scholars read it as an enacted parable about the temple; Jesus also draws a lesson on faith and prayer.
43381: When the fig tree puts out leaves, summer is near. The popular claim that the fig tree is modern Israel and its 'budding' was 1948 is a speculative dispensational reading; Luke says 'the fig tree and all the trees'.
43383: Jesus' knowledge amazes Nathanael. Some suggest he was studying Scripture there, as later rabbis spoke of studying under fig trees; this is speculative.
43384: Fig leaves in Eden (Gen 3:7), the fig tree declining kingship in Jotham's fable (Judg 9:10-11), a fig poultice for Hezekiah (Isa 38:21), loss of figs in judgement (Joel 1:7; Hab 3:17).
43385: Fruit by its tree (Jas 3:12), the cursed fig (Mark 11:13), the parable (Luke 13:6), lesson of the fig (Matt 24:32), stars falling like unripe figs (Rev 6:13).
43386: Mark notes 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13). This is part of what makes the act symbolic; it is not best read as an outburst of temper.
43389: The long-lived olive tree gave oil for food, light, medicine and anointing kings and priests. It stands for God's blessing, for Israel, and for the Spirit-anointed. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive branches grafted into Israel's tree.
43391: 'Messiah' (Hebrew mashiach) and 'Christ' (Greek christos) both mean 'anointed one', anointed with olive oil.
43393: Paul's point is humility: the root supports the branches. How this relates to the future of ethnic Israel is debated (see the Israel-and-church debate).
43395: A green olive in God's house; children like olive shoots; the olive leaf after the flood.
43396: The two olive trees: anointed witnesses
43397: In Zechariah, probably Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest. In Revelation, the two witnesses, read as the church's prophetic witness, as two end-time prophets, or as figures like Moses and Elijah.
43399: Oil for the lamp, for wounds and for prayer over the sick. Oil as a symbol of the Holy Spirit is a common Christian reading drawn from anointing; it is not stated directly.
43400: Promised land of olive oil (Deut 8:8), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:8-9), cherubim of olive wood in the temple (1 Kgs 6:23), gleanings left for the poor (Deut 24:20; Isa 17:6), the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:4).
43401: Gethsemane, whose name means 'oil press' (Matt 26:36), the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39; Acts 1:12), the good Samaritan's oil (Luke 10:34), the olive tree in Romans 11, two olive trees (Rev 11:4).
43402: The image of Jesus being 'pressed like olives' in Gethsemane is a devotional reflection on the name, not something the Gospels themselves draw out.
43405: The tall, fragrant, rot-resistant cedars of Lebanon were the finest building timber in the ancient Near East. Cedar stands for strength, majesty and pride: used for God's temple, a picture of the flourishing righteous, and an image of arrogant empires that God cuts down.
43407: David lives in a house of cedar while the ark is in a tent; Solomon's temple is lined with cedar.
43409: 'The righteous shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.'
43411: Assyria is a towering cedar felled. God's voice breaks the cedars.
43413: God takes a tender shoot from the top of the cedar and plants it on a high mountain, and birds nest in it. Many scholars see this behind Jesus' mustard-seed parable.
43415: Cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop were used together in purification. Perhaps chosen for durability or fragrance; the reason is not stated.
43416: Temple and palace building (1 Kgs 7:2), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:15), Jehoash's fable of thistle and cedar (2 Kgs 14:9), Solomon's botany from cedar to hyssop (1 Kgs 4:33), Jehoiakim's cedar palace condemned (Jer 22:14-15).
43417: Not mentioned by name in the NT; its imagery of birds nesting in a great tree echoes in the mustard-seed parable (Mark 4:32).
43418: Cedar's meaning flips between noble and arrogant. Read the context.
43420: Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a tiny mustard seed that grows into a large plant where birds nest, and says faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains. The point is small beginnings and surprising growth.
43421: The kingdom's small start and great end
43422: From a handful of Galilean disciples to a worldwide community.
43424: Birds nesting in a great tree was a known image for peoples under a kingdom. Most read the birds as nations, including Gentiles, coming into God's kingdom.
43426: Some interpreters (e.g. the *Scofield Reference Bible*) note that birds in the sower parable are the evil one and read the mustard tree as Christendom grown unnaturally large and harbouring evil. A minority view.
43427: Small faith in a great God
43428: The power is in God, not the size of the faith.
43429: Mustard is not named in the OT. The great-tree-with-birds image comes from Ezek 17:22-23, Ezek 31:6 and Dan 4:10-12.
43430: The parable (Mark 4:31), and faith like a mustard seed (Matt 17:20; Luke 17:6).
43431: 'Smallest of all seeds' is proverbial, not a botanical claim (orchid seeds are smaller). Mustard grows into a large shrub, not a true tree; Matthew and Luke's 'tree' may be a deliberate hint of Ezekiel's cedar, or a bit of humour about a humble garden plant.
43433: Wheat was the staple grain, so it stands for true fruit and for God's people. In Jesus' parable an enemy sows weeds, almost certainly darnel, which looks like wheat until it heads. The farmer lets both grow until the harvest, when they are separated. Chaff, the husk blown away, is a picture of the worthless.
43434: Good and evil growing together until the end
43435: Jesus explains: the field is the world, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the weeds the children of the evil one, the harvest the end of the age.
43437: Augustine used the parable against the Donatists to argue that the visible church contains both true and false members. Others note Jesus says the field is the world, not the church, and that discipline is still commanded. Debated.
43439: The winnowing fork separates grain from chaff.
43441: A grain of wheat must die to bear much fruit; Paul uses the seed for the resurrection body.
43443: Satan asks to sift the disciples like wheat.
43444: Wheat harvest and the Feast of Weeks (Exod 34:22), land of wheat and barley (Deut 8:8), Ruth gleaning (Ruth 2:23), chaff driven by wind (Ps 1:4), sowing the wind (Hos 8:7).
43445: Wheat and weeds (Matt 13:24-30), winnowing (Matt 3:12), the grain of wheat (John 12:24), sifting (Luke 22:31), the harvest of the earth (Rev 14:15-16).
43446: The parable warns against premature uprooting by human servants; it is not a denial that churches should exercise any discipline.
43448: Thorns come into the story with the curse on the ground after the fall. They picture frustration, judgement, worthless people and the cares that choke faith. At the cross, soldiers crown Jesus with thorns, and many Christians see him bearing the curse.
43449: The curse on work and the ground
43450: Isaiah promises that instead of the thorn will come up the cypress.
43451: Crown of thorns: mock kingship and the curse borne
43452: The soldiers mean mockery. Connecting the thorns to the curse of Gen 3 is an ancient Christian reflection, not stated in the Gospels.
43453: Worries and riches that choke the word
43456: Remaining Canaanites will be thorns in Israel's sides.
43458: Greek skolops can mean a stake. Suggestions include poor eyesight, chronic illness, persecution, opponents (cf. Num 33:55) or temptation. No consensus.
43459: The curse (Gen 3:18), the burning bush, which was a thorn bush (Exod 3:2), Gideon's thorn-threshing (Judg 8:7), the bramble king (Judg 9:14-15), the vineyard overrun (Isa 5:6), thorns on the pagan altars (Hos 10:8).
43460: Grapes not gathered from thorns (Matt 7:16), the sower (Matt 13:7), the crown (John 19:2), Paul's thorn (2 Cor 12:7), land bearing thorns (Heb 6:8).
43461: The ram 'caught in a thicket' (Gen 22:13) is sometimes linked to the crown of thorns. That is a devotional typology, not something the NT draws.
43463: Hyssop was a small, bushy herb (probably Syrian marjoram) used as a brush to sprinkle blood or water in rites of cleansing. It shows up at the first Passover, in David's prayer 'purge me with hyssop', and at the cross.
43465: Hyssop dipped in the Passover lamb's blood marked the doorposts.
43467: Used for cleansing skin disease, houses and corpse-impurity.
43469: David asks for the purification only God can give.
43471: Only John mentions hyssop (Mark and Matthew say 'a reed'). Many see a deliberate Passover link. A sprig of hyssop seems too weak to lift a sponge, so some have proposed a different Greek word (hyssos, javelin), found in one late manuscript. Debated.
43473: Solomon's knowledge reached from the cedar to the hyssop on the wall, that is, from greatest to smallest.
43474: Passover (Exod 12:22), cleansing rites (Lev 14; Num 19), David's prayer (Ps 51:7), Solomon's botany (1 Kgs 4:33).
43475: The cross (John 19:29) and Hebrews' summary of covenant sprinkling (Heb 9:19).
43476: The plant called hyssop today (Hyssopus officinalis) is probably not the biblical one.
43478: The biblical 'lily' is an unidentified bright flower, possibly the lotus, anemone or iris. It stands for beauty, love and God's lavish care. Jesus says to consider how the lilies grow: not even Solomon was dressed like one of them.
43480: Wild flowers, here today and burned tomorrow, are dressed by God; how much more his children.
43482: In Song 2:1 the woman most likely speaks ('I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys'). Applying it to Christ is a later devotional tradition.
43486: Lily-work topped the pillars and the rim of the bronze sea, suggesting Eden-like beauty in God's house.
43488: Medieval art made the white lily a sign of Mary's purity, and Easter lilies are a modern custom. Tradition, not biblical symbolism.
43489: Song of Songs (Song 2:1; Song 5:13), Hosea (Hos 14:5), temple pillars (1 Kgs 7:19), and psalm titles set 'to Lilies' (for example Ps 45 and Ps 69), probably a tune name.
43490: Only in Jesus' saying about the lilies of the field (Matt 6:28; Luke 12:27).
43491: Exact flower identifications are uncertain. Do not build meaning on modern varieties like the white Easter lily.
43493: The date palm was a tree of oases and abundance, and its branches were waved at festivals and victories. Crowds wave palm branches as Jesus enters Jerusalem, and the redeemed in Revelation hold palms before God's throne.
43495: Palm branches were part of the booths and rejoicing at the Feast of Tabernacles.
43497: Palms had been waved for the Maccabean liberators (1 and 2 Maccabees) and appeared on Jewish coins; the crowd hails Jesus as a national king. In Revelation they mark the victory of the redeemed.
43498: 'The righteous flourish like the palm tree.'
43500: Carved palms with cherubim and flowers made the sanctuary a garden of God's presence.
43502: Christian art gave martyrs the palm of victory, and the church remembers the triumphal entry on Palm Sunday. Tradition.
43503: Elim's seventy palms (Exod 15:27), Jericho the city of palms (Deut 34:3), Deborah judging under her palm (Judg 4:5), the name Tamar (Gen 38:6; 2 Sam 13:1), idols 'upright as the palm' (Jer 10:5).
43504: Triumphal entry (John 12:13) and the great multitude (Rev 7:9).
43505: Only John mentions palms specifically at the entry; the other Gospels speak of branches and cloaks.
43508: The almond is the first tree to blossom in Israel's late winter, so its Hebrew name shaqed sounds like 'the watcher' or 'wakeful one'. Aaron's dead staff budded, blossomed and bore almonds overnight to show God's choice of priest, and the tabernacle lampstand had almond-shaped cups.
43510: Twelve staffs were laid before the LORD; only Aaron's came to life. It was kept before the ark as a sign against rebels.
43512: A wordplay: Jeremiah sees an almond branch (shaqed) and God says he is watching (shoqed) to perform his word.
43513: Light and life in the sanctuary
43514: The lampstand's cups were shaped like almond blossoms, making it a stylised flowering tree. Many see an echo of the tree of life.
43516: 'The almond tree blossoms' probably pictures white hair. Debated but widely held.
43518: Fathers saw the dead rod blooming as a figure of Christ's resurrection; others made it a type of the virgin birth (life from what could not naturally bear). Both are tradition.
43519: Gift of almonds to Joseph (Gen 43:11), Jacob's rods (Gen 30:37, where 'hazel' in KJV is probably almond, luz), the lampstand (Exod 25:33), Aaron's rod (Num 17:8), Jeremiah's vision (Jer 1:11), old age (Eccl 12:5).
43520: Only Heb 9:4, listing Aaron's budded rod in the ark.
43521: Hebrew wordplay (shaqed and shoqed) is the key to Jeremiah 1; English readers can easily miss it and look for symbolism elsewhere.
43523: The tree of life stood in the middle of Eden. After the fall, humans were barred from it. It returns at the end of the Bible, beside the river in the new Jerusalem, bearing fruit every month, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Between those, Proverbs uses it for wisdom and righteous living.
43525: Barring the way can be read as judgement and as mercy (not living forever in a fallen state). Both readings appear in Jewish and Christian tradition.
43526: Restored access in the new creation
43527: The paradise of God is open again. Some manuscripts of Rev 22:19 read 'book of life' (KJV) instead of 'tree of life'; most modern texts read 'tree'.
43529: Wisdom, the fruit of righteousness, fulfilled longing and gentle speech are each 'a tree of life'.
43530: The cross as tree of life
43531: The NT calls the cross a 'tree' (xylon). Early and medieval Christians linked it to the tree of life: the curse that came by a tree is undone by a tree. Tradition.
43532: The lampstand as a stylised tree
43533: Some scholars think the menorah, with branches and almond blossoms, recalls the tree of life in the sanctuary.
43534: Eden (Gen 2-3), Proverbs (Prov 3:18), the river of healing trees (Ezek 47:12), the righteous like a tree by streams (Ps 1:3).
43535: Promise to the victorious at Ephesus (Rev 2:7) and the city's tree with twelve fruits (Rev 22:2).
43536: Kabbalah's 'tree of life' diagram is a much later mystical system and should not be read back into Genesis.
43538: Olive oil was food, medicine, lamp fuel and cosmetic in Israel. Because it was poured on kings, priests and sacred objects to set them apart for God, it became a picture of being chosen and equipped by God, and of joy and healing.
43539: Consecration: set apart for God's service
43540: A special holy anointing oil was mixed for the tabernacle and priests and was forbidden for ordinary use. Pouring oil on a person marked them as God's chosen servant.
43541: Association with the Spirit of God
43542: When Samuel anointed David, the Spirit came on him from that day. Isaiah links being anointed with having the Spirit, and Jesus applies this to himself. The Bible links oil and Spirit closely but never states a formula that oil equals the Spirit.
43544: Oil on the head was a sign of festivity and welcome; the 'oil of joy' replaces mourning.
43546: Oil was ordinary first-aid. In James, elders anoint the sick with prayer; whether the oil is medicinal, symbolic or sacramental is debated between traditions.
43547: Oil appears in daily life (bread, lamps, skin) and in worship: grain offerings were mixed with it, the lampstand burned it, and kings, priests and the tabernacle were anointed with it. A full supply of oil is a sign of covenant blessing (Deut 7:13), and its loss a sign of judgement.
43548: The title Christ (Greek christos) means 'anointed one'. Jesus is said to be anointed with the Spirit rather than with literal oil, and believers share an 'anointing' from God (2 Cor 1:21; 1 John 2:20). The disciples and later the elders used oil with prayer for the sick.
43549: In the parable of the ten virgins (Matt 25:1-13) the oil is often read as the Holy Spirit, good works or genuine faith; the parable itself does not say, so hold any single reading loosely. Modern talk of 'the anointing' as a transferable power goes beyond what these texts state.
43553: Bread was the basic food of the ancient world, so it stands for life itself and for God's daily provision. Jesus took this ordinary food and called himself 'the bread of life', and gave bread to his followers as a sign of his body.
43555: Manna in the wilderness taught Israel to depend on God one day at a time; the Lord's Prayer asks for 'daily bread'.
43557: People do not live by bread alone but by every word from God; a 'famine of hearing the word' is worse than a food famine.
43558: Jesus as the bread of life
43559: Jesus contrasts himself with the manna: whoever comes to him will not hunger. How far John 6 refers to the Lord's Supper is debated.
43561: Twelve loaves (the 'bread of the Presence') lay before God in the holy place. At the Last Supper bread signifies Christ's body, and 'one loaf' expresses the unity of the church.
43563: At Passover Israel ate bread without yeast because they left Egypt in a hurry; Paul applies this to removing 'old leaven' of malice from the church.
43564: Bread is hospitality (Gen 18:5-6), wages, sacrifice and provision. Manna, the bread of the Presence and the feast of Unleavened Bread give bread a central place in Israel's worship and memory.
43565: Jesus feeds crowds with a few loaves, teaches his disciples to ask for daily bread, calls himself the bread of life, and institutes the Lord's Supper with bread. The early church 'broke bread' together.
43566: What exactly the bread of the Lord's Supper is (Christ's body really present, a spiritual presence, or a memorial sign) is one of the major debates of church history; see /debates/lords-supper.
43571: Wine in the Bible is a gift that gladdens people and a sign of God's abundant blessing, especially at feasts. It is also a warning image: drunkenness ruins people, and God's judgement is pictured as a cup of wine that makes nations stagger.
43573: Plentiful grain, wine and oil is the standard picture of a blessed land.
43575: The prophets picture the coming age as a feast with the finest wine; Jesus' first sign is turning water into a huge quantity of good wine at a wedding.
43577: At the Last Supper the cup of wine signifies Christ's blood poured out for forgiveness.
43579: Judgement is a strong wine that makes the nations stagger, or a winepress in which grapes are trodden.
43581: Drunkenness is consistently condemned; Paul contrasts being drunk with wine and being filled with the Spirit.
43582: Wine is part of offerings (Num 15:5), feasts and ordinary meals. Nazirites and priests on duty abstained (Num 6:3; Lev 10:9). Israel is pictured as God's vineyard, and its failure as sour grapes (Isa 5:1-7).
43583: Jesus drinks wine and is accused of being a drunkard by his critics (Matt 11:19). New wine needs new wineskins (Mark 2:22), a picture of the newness of the kingdom. The cup of the Lord's Supper holds wine.
43584: Biblical wine was fermented and could make people drunk. Some Christians argue that 'new wine' or diluted wine differs from modern alcohol and favour abstinence; others hold moderate drinking is permitted. The texts condemn drunkenness clearly; total abstinence is a debated application.
43588: A cup is what someone is given to drink, so it came to mean the experience or destiny God hands to a person: blessing for some, judgement for others. Jesus called his coming suffering 'the cup'.
43590: The LORD is David's 'cup'; his cup overflows with good things.
43592: Nations who oppose God must drink a cup that makes them stagger.
43594: In Gethsemane Jesus prays for the cup to pass but accepts it. Many read this as Jesus taking the cup of wrath meant for others; others stress suffering and martyrdom more broadly.
43596: The cup of the Lord's Supper is a 'cup of blessing' and the new covenant in Christ's blood.
43597: Cups appear at meals and in the Passover-like thanksgiving of the Psalms, and as a common prophetic image for judgement on Judah and the nations.
43598: Jesus takes the cup at the Last Supper, prays about 'this cup' in Gethsemane, and asks James and John if they can drink his cup. Revelation pictures Babylon holding a golden cup of abominations (Rev 17:4) and receiving God's cup of wrath.
43599: The Passover meal in later Jewish practice has four cups; linking specific Gospel cups to these (for example Luke 22:17 and 22:20) is a common suggestion, but the rabbinic order is documented later than the New Testament, so treat it as possible rather than certain.
43601: Salt preserved food, gave it flavour and was part of making agreements by sharing a meal. So it stands for lasting covenant loyalty and for the good influence God's people should have. Salted land, on the other hand, was barren, so salt can also mean judgement.
43603: Offerings were to be salted with 'the salt of the covenant'; a 'covenant of salt' means one that is permanent.
43605: Jesus calls his followers the salt of the earth and warns against losing saltiness. Whether he means preservation, flavour, or both is debated; the text does not specify.
43607: Speech 'seasoned with salt' is attractive and thoughtful.
43609: Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt; a land 'sown with salt' is ruined.
43611: Elisha heals Jericho's water with salt; newborns were rubbed with salt.
43612: Salt is required in offerings, describes unbreakable covenants, and marks both healing (Elisha) and devastation (Sodom, Abimelech's Shechem). The Dead Sea is called the Salt Sea (Gen 14:3).
43613: Jesus' 'salt of the earth' saying, his puzzling 'everyone will be salted with fire' (Mark 9:49), and Paul's advice on speech.
43614: Ancient salt from the Dead Sea area was often mixed with other minerals and could lose its taste as the salt leached out; that explains Jesus' image better than modern pure table salt.
